blocks.text: A surgeon removes two-thirds of a donor's liver, and within weeks the remaining liver has regrown to near its original size. A patient who has a myocardial infarction, however, is left with a permanent white scar in the heart wall. Both tissues were injured, but one regenerates and the other repairs by scarring.

blocks.markdown: After injury, tissues can heal in two ways. **Regeneration** replaces lost cells with the same cell type, restoring normal structure and function. **Repair (healing by scarring)** replaces lost tissue with connective tissue, which restores continuity but not function. The route depends on the proliferative capacity of the cells and on whether the tissue framework (extracellular matrix scaffold) is intact.

blocks.title: Labile, stable and permanent cells
blocks.text: Labile cells divide continuously throughout life and replace cells that are lost (surface epithelia, bone marrow haemopoietic cells). Stable (quiescent) cells have low turnover but can divide on demand after injury (hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, fibroblasts, endothelium). Permanent cells have left the cell cycle and cannot divide in adult life (neurons, cardiac myocytes), so injury is repaired by scar.

rows: Hepatocytes, proximal tubule cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle
Regeneration if scaffold intact; otherwise scar
Scar (glial scar in brain, fibrous scar in heart)
blocks.caption: Classification of tissue cells by regenerative capacity.

blocks.markdown:
### Stages of repair

When regeneration is not possible, repair proceeds as follows.

1. **Haemostasis and inflammation** (immediate to days): platelets form a plug; fibrin clot supplies a provisional matrix; neutrophils then macrophages clear debris.
2. **Proliferation** (days 3 to 14): macrophages release growth factors (TGF-beta, VEGF, PDGF, FGF). **Granulation tissue** forms: new capillaries (**angiogenesis**), proliferating fibroblasts and loose extracellular matrix. It is pink, soft and granular on the surface. Epithelial cells migrate across the wound, re-epithelialising it.
3. **Remodelling and maturation** (weeks to months): fibroblasts deposit type III collagen then replace it with stronger **type I collagen**; matrix metalloproteinases remodel the matrix. Capillaries regress, fibroblasts become sparse and the **scar** becomes pale and avascular with increasing tensile strength.

blocks.latex: \text{wound strength (\%)} = \frac{\text{tensile strength of wound}}{\text{tensile strength of unwounded skin}} \times 100
blocks.caption: Wound strength is expressed relative to normal skin. It is about 10% at the end of the first week and plateaus near 70-80% of normal.

blocks.markdown:
### Primary and secondary intention

**Healing by primary intention** occurs when wound edges are closely apposed (clean surgical incision, sutured). The wound space is small, the clot is thin, only minimal granulation tissue is needed, and the result is a thin scar. **Healing by secondary intention** occurs when there is a large tissue defect, as in an ulcer, an infarct or a large open wound. More fibrin and necrotic debris must be cleared; much more granulation tissue forms; **wound contraction** by **myofibroblasts** reduces the defect size; and the scar is larger.

blocks.title: Timeline of a sutured incision
blocks.prompt: A surgeon closes a 10 cm abdominal incision with sutures. Describe what the tissue contains at 24 hours, day 5 and 6 weeks.

steps.text: At 24 hours the incision is filled with a blood clot containing fibrin. Neutrophils infiltrate and the edges begin to show epithelial thickening.
By day 5 granulation tissue (new capillaries and fibroblasts) fills the incision with type III collagen; macrophages replace neutrophils; epithelium has bridged the defect.

By 6 weeks fibroblast numbers have fallen, type III collagen has been replaced by type I and the scar is largely acellular and pale. Strength continues to rise but never completely reaches that of normal skin.

blocks.answer: Clot and neutrophils, then granulation tissue with type III collagen, then a mature collagen scar with type I collagen.

blocks.markdown:
### Maturation of granulation tissue into scar

Granulation tissue is vascular, rich in fibroblasts and loosely arranged type III collagen. As growth factor signalling declines, apoptosis removes many capillaries and fibroblasts. Fibroblasts continue to secrete collagen and matrix metalloproteinases remodel it, cross-linking and re-orienting fibres along lines of stress. **Myofibroblasts** shrink the wound. The result is a dense, relatively acellular collagenous scar, with few vessels. Scar tissue lacks skin appendages and elastic fibres and never regains full original strength.

blocks.title: Which tissue regenerates?
blocks.prompt: Predict the healing outcome for a 2 cm injury to (a) the small intestine mucosa, (b) a liver after partial hepatectomy with intact lobule architecture, (c) the left ventricular myocardium.

steps.text: (a) Intestinal epithelium is labile, with stem cells in the crypts: full regeneration.
(b) Hepatocytes are stable cells; if the architecture and scaffold are retained they re-enter the cell cycle: regeneration.
(c) Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells and cannot divide: the defect is filled by granulation tissue and then a fibrous scar.

items: Granulation tissue is not the same as a granuloma.
Type III collagen predominates early; type I collagen in the mature scar.
Myofibroblasts are the cells of wound contraction.
TGF-beta is the principal driver of fibrosis and matrix deposition.

blocks.title: Do not confuse granulation tissue with a granuloma
blocks.text: Granulation tissue is new vascular connective tissue formed during healing. A granuloma is a focal collection of activated macrophages in chronic inflammation. The words sound alike but the entities are unrelated.

points: Labile cells divide continuously, stable cells divide on demand, and permanent cells cannot divide, which determines whether tissue regenerates or scars.

Wound healing proceeds through haemostasis and inflammation, granulation tissue formation and remodelling; primary intention has minimal granulation tissue and secondary intention has abundant tissue and contraction.
Granulation tissue matures into a scar as capillaries regress and type III collagen is replaced by cross-linked type I collagen.

questions.stem: Cardiac myocytes are classified as which type of cell population?

distractorRationale.c: Stable cells such as hepatocytes divide on demand.
distractorRationale.d: Cardiac myocytes are terminally differentiated, not stem cells.

questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes have left the cell cycle and cannot meaningfully regenerate, so injury results in scarring. This differs from labile and stable populations.

questions.stem: Which cell type is classified as labile?

options.text: Epithelial cells of the small intestine

questions.correctOptionText: Epithelial cells of the small intestine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: intestinal epithelium is continuously renewed.

questions.explanation: Surface epithelia and haemopoietic cells divide continuously and are labile. Hepatocytes are stable, whereas neurons and cardiac myocytes are permanent.

questions.stem: A farmer has a large, deep, gaping laceration that is left to heal without suturing. Which finding is characteristic of this type of healing?

options.text: Abundant granulation tissue with wound contraction by myofibroblasts
Minimal granulation tissue and a thin scar

questions.correctOptionText: Abundant granulation tissue with wound contraction by myofibroblasts

distractorRationale.c: Skin dermis cannot regenerate fully, leaving a scar.
distractorRationale.d: Inflammation is present in all healing.

questions.explanation: An open wound with a large defect heals by secondary intention, which requires abundant granulation tissue and myofibroblast contraction. The scar is larger than after a sutured wound.

questions.stem: Which collagen type predominates in early granulation tissue and is later replaced in the mature scar?

options.text: Type III replaced by type I
Type I replaced by type III
Type II replaced by type IV
Type IV replaced by type II

questions.correctOptionText: Type III replaced by type I

distractorRationale.d: Type IV is basement membrane collagen.

questions.explanation: Fibroblasts initially lay down type III collagen, which is weaker. During remodelling, it is replaced by cross-linked type I collagen that gives tensile strength.

questions.stem: True or false: Granulation tissue is characterised by new capillaries, proliferating fibroblasts and loose matrix, and is a feature of repair rather than of granulomatous inflammation.
questions.explanation: Granulation tissue is the proliferative stage of repair. It is distinct from a granuloma, which is a collection of activated macrophages.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has a large myocardial infarct. After 6 weeks, the damaged area has become pale and firm. Which sequence best describes what happened?

options.text: Dead myocytes cleared by macrophages, granulation tissue formed, then collagenous scar as capillaries regressed
Surviving myocytes divided to replace the dead cells exactly
Neutrophils persisted and formed an abscess

questions.correctOptionText: Dead myocytes cleared by macrophages, granulation tissue formed, then collagenous scar as capillaries regressed

distractorRationale.d: No such cell type exists in the heart.

questions.explanation: Myocytes cannot regenerate, so macrophages clear necrotic cells and granulation tissue forms. Over weeks it matures into a pale collagenous scar.

questions.stem: A surgical wound in the skin has a tensile strength of 20 N when tested at 6 weeks. Unwounded skin of the same site has a tensile strength of 25 N. Calculate the wound strength as a percentage of normal.
questions.explanation: Relative strength = 20/25 x 100 = 80%. This agrees with the general principle that even a mature scar reaches only about 70-80% of the strength of unwounded skin.

questions.stem: A skin ulcer has an initial area of 12 cm^2 and contracts by myofibroblast action to 3 cm^2. Calculate the percentage reduction in wound area by contraction.
questions.explanation: The reduction is (12 - 3)/12 = 0.75, i.e. 75%. Contraction is characteristic of secondary intention healing and is performed by myofibroblasts.

questions.stem: Explain why a liver injured by acute toxin exposure can recover its structure, while a myocardial infarct heals by scarring.
markingGuide: Hepatocytes are stable cells that can re-enter the cell cycle
Regeneration is possible if the connective tissue scaffold (lobule architecture) is intact
Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells and cannot divide
Defect in the heart filled by granulation tissue then fibrous scar
Labile cells also regenerate; classification explains the difference
questions.explanation: Healing depends on the proliferative capacity of the cell type and intact stroma. Stable hepatocytes regenerate, permanent myocytes do not.

questions.stem: Contrast healing by primary and secondary intention, then describe how granulation tissue matures into a scar.
markingGuide: Primary: apposed edges, minimal granulation tissue, thin scar, little contraction
Secondary: large defect, abundant granulation tissue, marked contraction by myofibroblasts, larger scar
Granulation tissue: new capillaries, fibroblasts, type III collagen
Maturation: capillary regression and fibroblast apoptosis, type III replaced by type I collagen, cross-linking
Result is a pale, avascular, acellular scar of strength less than normal
questions.explanation: The amount of tissue to be filled determines the type of healing. Maturation reduces vascularity and cellularity while collagen type and cross-linking increase strength.
